slides.source: Source: Blender manual, Modeling, Introduction and Scene Layout, Collections.

OBJECT MODE: SELECT AND MOVE THE WHOLE OBJECT
Object Mode treats the cube as one object: one move changes the location, the mesh is untouched.

slides.title: Mesh, vertex, edge and face
slides.source: Source: Chapter 3, "Apply transforms"; glossary, 3D assets and Blender.
slides.notes: V, E and F are counted in code from the face list. The check V minus E plus F equals 2 holds for any closed mesh without holes.
slides.picture: A cube slowly turning. First solid, then its 8 vertices as dots, its 12 edges as red lines, its 6 faces tinted, with the count shown.

new_texts: The vertices, edges and faces that make a 3D shape; the chapter calls it mesh data.
A mesh is the shape's points, lines and surfaces.
A mesh is what the chapter means by mesh data: the points that carry the real size.
all_texts: The vertices, edges and faces that make a 3D shape; the chapter calls it mesh data.
A mesh is the shape's points, lines and surfaces.
A mesh is what the chapter means by mesh data: the points that carry the real size.

new_texts: A corner point of a mesh.
Every corner is one vertex. A cube has 8.

new_texts: Edges join vertices. Count them once each: 12.

slides.title: Quads, triangles and the polygon count
slides.source: Source: glossary, 3D assets and Blender (Quad, Triangle versus face versus vertex count); Chapter 3, low-poly prop.
slides.notes: Counts computed from the face list: triangles = sum over faces of (corners minus 2).
slides.picture: A square split by a diagonal into two triangles, and a cube with a diagonal on each face. Then four bars: faces, triangles, vertices, GPU vertices.

new_texts: A face with 4 vertices adds 4 − 2 = 2 triangles.
A quad is a four-sided face. The GPU draws triangles, so each quad is split in two.
all_texts: A face with 4 vertices adds 4 − 2 = 2 triangles.
A quad is a four-sided face. The GPU draws triangles, so each quad is split in two.

new_texts: Three tallies of one mesh: engines budget by triangles, Blender shows faces, and vertices are split where UVs or normals differ.
FOUR TALLIES OF THE SAME CUBE
Hard edges split a vertex per face: 6 × 4 = 24.
One mesh, four numbers. Ask which one a budget uses before you compare models.
all_texts: Three tallies of one mesh: engines budget by triangles, Blender shows faces, and vertices are split where UVs or normals differ.
FOUR TALLIES OF THE SAME CUBE

slides.title: Normals and flipped normals
slides.source: Source: glossary, 3D assets and Blender (Normal, Flipped normals).
slides.notes: A 12-sided cross-section stands in for a mesh. Brightness is the dot product of the normal and the direction to the light.
slides.picture: A 12-sided cross-section with an arrow out of each face and light from the upper left. Faces turned to the light are bright. Then the normals of three bright faces flip and those faces go dark.

new_texts: Faces lit by the light: 6 of 12
The normal is the arrow out of the face. Light and culling both use it to decide what the face looks like.
all_texts: Faces lit by the light: 6 of 12
The normal is the arrow out of the face. Light and culling both use it to decide what the face looks like.

new_texts: Faces pointing inward, so they look dark or vanish.
Faces lit by the light: 3 of 12 (3 flipped)
Flip a normal and the face looks away from the light, so it looks dark, or is not drawn at all.
all_texts: Faces pointing inward, so they look dark or vanish.
Faces lit by the light: 3 of 12 (3 flipped)

slides.picture: A square moving, turning and growing on a grid. Then two posts placed at height zero, one with its origin in the middle and one at its base. Then a bar turned 60 degrees about its middle and about its end.

where the object is measured from
what a turn or stretch happens around
TOP VIEW: X TO THE RIGHT, Y UP, 1 SQUARE = 1 UNIT
The transform is three things on the object: location, rotation, scale. The mesh itself is not touched.

slides.title: Apply transforms, local and global space
slides.source: Source: Chapter 3, "Apply transforms"; glossary, 3D assets and Blender (Apply transforms, Scale versus size); Blender manual, Transform Orientations.
slides.notes: Numbers (0.1, 0.1, 0.9) and a 2 m cube are the chapter example. The size you see is scale times mesh size, computed.
slides.picture: A table of scale, mesh size and size you see for a pole, before and after apply; the size you see does not change. Then a point at fixed local coordinates whose global coordinates change as the parent turns.

new_texts: Bake position, rotation and scale into the mesh and reset them to neutral.
The pole looks the same either way.
Only the mesh now carries the size.
Scaling a 2 m cube to (0.1, 0.1, 0.9) makes a pole, but the mesh is still 2 m. Apply puts 0.2 × 0.2 × 1.8 m in the mesh.
all_texts: Bake position, rotation and scale into the mesh and reset them to neutral.
The pole looks the same either way.
Only the mesh now carries the size.
Scaling a 2 m cube to (0.1, 0.1, 0.9) makes a pole, but the mesh is still 2 m. Apply puts 0.2 × 0.2 × 1.8 m in the mesh.

new_texts: Local coordinates are measured from the object's origin; global ones from the scene's.
PARENT TURNS; LOCAL POINT STAYS PUT
A point has two sets of numbers. Local ones stay put; global ones change when the parent moves or turns.
all_texts: Bake position, rotation and scale into the mesh and reset them to neutral.
Local coordinates are measured from the object's origin; global ones from the scene's.
PARENT TURNS; LOCAL POINT STAYS PUT

slides.title: Units and the right-handed +Z up axes
slides.source: Source: Chapter 3, "Units" and "Axes"; glossary, 3D assets and Blender (Unit).
slides.notes: The 2.1 m player capsule and 1.8 m post are from Chapter 3. Reading 1 unit as 0.01 m is an invented wrong case to show the size error.
slides.picture: Two bars, a 2.1 metre player and a 1.8 unit post, with the post shrinking to 1.8 centimetres if a unit is read as a centimetre. Then the post upright in Blender and lying on its side in Godot until the exporter converts the axes.

new_texts: The length one coordinate step stands for (usually a metre).
A 1.8 UNIT POST NEXT TO THE 2.1 M PLAYER
Dashed: the post at 1 unit = 1 m.
One unit is one metre in Blender, glTF and Godot, so nothing converts. Read a unit as a centimetre and the post is 100 times too small.
all_texts: The length one coordinate step stands for (usually a metre).
A 1.8 UNIT POST NEXT TO THE 2.1 M PLAYER
Dashed: the post at 1 unit = 1 m.
One unit is one metre in Blender, glTF and Godot, so nothing converts. Read a unit as a centimetre and the post is 100 times too small.

new_texts: Blender: X cross Y gives Z, and Z is up. glTF and Godot put +Y up.
Blender is right-handed, Z up. Godot is Y up. The exporter's +Y Up option puts Z extent 1.8 on Godot's Y; without it the post lies down.
all_texts: The length one coordinate step stands for (usually a metre).

slides.title: Modifiers: mirror, subdivision, bevel
slides.source: Source: Chapter 3, export "apply modifiers"; Blender manual, Modeling, Modifiers.
slides.notes: Subdivision counts: faces times 4 per level on an all-quad mesh. Vertex count V+E+F per level.
slides.picture: A base mesh, a modifier and a result. Then a half shape mirrored into a whole. Then a square cut into more corners at each level with face counts. Then a square with its corners bevelled in 0 to 3 segments.

new_texts: A live step that changes a mesh without editing it.
bakes the result into the mesh
Here the modifier is Subdivision Surface, level 1.
Switch it off: the result is the base mesh again.
A modifier is a step in a stack. The base mesh never changes, so you can reorder or switch steps off.
all_texts: A live step that changes a mesh without editing it.
bakes the result into the mesh
Here the modifier is Subdivision Surface, level 1.
Switch it off: the result is the base mesh again.
A modifier is a step in a stack. The base mesh never changes, so you can reorder or switch steps off.

new_texts: Copies the mesh across an axis, so you model one half.
MODEL THE RIGHT HALF; MIRROR ON X
You model 5 vertices; the shape has 8.
Mirror copies across x = 0. You build and edit one half; both sides always match.
all_texts: A live step that changes a mesh without editing it.
Copies the mesh across an axis, so you model one half.
bakes the result into the mesh
MODEL THE RIGHT HALF; MIRROR ON X
You model 5 vertices; the shape has 8.
Mirror copies across x = 0. You build and edit one half; both sides always match.

new_texts: Splits and smooths faces; each level makes 4 times as many.
ONE FACE'S OUTLINE, THEN 2× THE CORNERS PER LEVEL
Each subdivision level multiplies the faces of an all-quad mesh by 4: 6, 24, 96. Watch the triangle budget.

A SQUARE CORNER, CUT IN 0 TO 3 SEGMENTS
A sharp edge has no width, so it cannot catch a highlight. A bevel gives it one, for the cost of more vertices.
Bevel adds corners. More segments give a rounder edge and more vertices.

slides.title: UV maps, unwrapping, materials and textures
slides.source: Source: glossary, 3D assets and Blender (UV map, Unwrapping, Material versus texture); glossary, Textures and materials.
slides.notes: Seam count is computed: 12 cube edges minus 5 edges kept joined in the cross layout. Material values are illustrative.
slides.picture: A cube beside its cross-shaped UV layout, with matching face tones. Then the faces flying from the cube to the layout with the cut edges in red. Then a material card with its settings and an image slot filled by a checker texture.

new_texts: The flattened 2D layout of a mesh used to place a texture.
CUBE FACES ↔ CELLS OF THE UV MAP
6 faces, 6 cells. Each cell is where that face reads the texture.
The UV map gives every face a place on the image. U and V are the 2D axes of that image.
all_texts: The flattened 2D layout of a mesh used to place a texture.
CUBE FACES ↔ CELLS OF THE UV MAP
6 faces, 6 cells. Each cell is where that face reads the texture.
The UV map gives every face a place on the image. U and V are the 2D axes of that image.

new_texts: Cutting a mesh and flattening it into a UV map.
Red: cuts (seams). 12 edges − 5 kept joined = 7 seams.
Unwrapping cuts the mesh along seams so it can lie flat. A cube cut as a cross keeps 5 edges joined and cuts 7.

slides.title: Before you hand a model to the game
slides.picture: A checklist of six items drawn one at a time.

Is the scene in metres, with unit scale 1.0?
Is the transform applied, so scale reads (1, 1, 1)?
Do all normals point out, so no face is dark or missing?
Is the triangle count within budget after the modifiers run?
Is it unwrapped, and does each material have the name the game expects?
Then say it exactly: not “fix the scale”, but “apply rotation and scale, then check it reads (1, 1, 1)”.
